blocks.text: Dear Ms. Gonzalez:

I am writing to set down, as carefully as I can, the terms on which our firm would take up the organization design work you and your colleagues have described to us over the past several weeks, so that once you have read this letter and, if it records the understanding we reached, returned a signed copy to me, there is one document either of us can turn to should a question later arise about what we agreed. I have tried throughout to promise only what I am confident we can deliver, and if any sentence here reads as claiming more than that, I would rather you raised it with me before you sign than let it stand.
The Assignment as We Understand It

As we understand it, {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} has grown to a point where the way the organization is structured, the way responsibilities are divided among its managers, and the way decisions travel through it all deserve a considered look from outside the business. You have asked us to examine the operating structure as it stands today, the roles and reporting relationships that compose it, the spans and layers through which the work is directed, and the points at which authority for a decision is either unclear or lodged in the wrong place, and to return to you with a design you can act on. Our work will move from an orderly reading of how the organization is run today, through a view of where the present structure helps the business and where it holds it back, to a set of recommendations on the structure, the roles, and the decision rights a revised model would call for. What the engagement does not take in is the running of your operation, which stays entirely yours to direct, nor legal or accounting advice, on which you should keep relying on the advisers who ordinarily give it; where our analysis touches those matters we offer a reasoned business view and not a professional opinion in their place.
How We Would Approach the Work

Our way of working is deliberate, and I hope you will find it plain rather than clever. We begin by listening, to you and to the managers who already carry a working sense of how the organization actually runs, and only then do we set down the few judgments an organization design truly turns on and build the analysis outward from them, so that every recommendation we eventually put in front of you can be traced back to the evidence beneath it. Where that evidence will support a firm recommendation we will give you one, and where it will support only a range or a caution we will tell you so instead, because a recommendation that runs past what we actually know is of no use to you and no credit to us.
The People You Would Be Working With

I will keep my own hand on the engagement and read anything of consequence before it leaves us under the firm's name, but the daily work would rest with two of our people I would ask you to come to know. Julie Parks, a Senior Engagement Manager, would run the engagement day to day, turn the scope set out in this letter into a workable plan, and be your point of contact from the first meeting through to the close. Deborah Gordon, an Associate, would carry the analysis and build the exhibits on which the recommendations rest; she keeps her work close to the evidence, so that a question about any figure can be answered from its source rather than from memory. You are welcome to reach me at any time, though for most day-to-day matters Julie Parks will be the quicker route to an answer.
Fee and Commencement

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is {{fact:f:E-2011-002.fee}}, which covers the time of the people named above through the completion of the work and against which we will render invoices as the engagement proceeds. We would begin the work on {{fact:f:E-2011-002.start}}, and would move into the first interviews and information requests promptly after that, so that the opening weeks are not lost to arranging what could have been settled in advance.
Invoicing and Payment

Each invoice we render against the fee stated above is payable within thirty days of your receipt of it. The fee covers our people and their time, and not the incidental costs of the work, such as travel or the reproduction of materials, which we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us and nothing more. Should the shape of the work change materially from what this letter contemplates, I will raise the fee with you and we will settle it together before any further work is done, so that nothing ever reaches you on an invoice as a surprise.
Duration and Ending the Engagement

We expect the engagement to run for something on the order of five months, though I would ask you to treat that as an honest estimate of the work rather than a promise about the calendar, since we will regard the assignment as finished when it is genuinely done and not merely when a set number of weeks has passed. Either of us may bring the engagement to an end on thirty days' written notice to the other, and should you choose to do so you would owe us for the work properly performed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and for nothing beyond that.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use only for the purposes of the engagement. That obligation binds every member of the team, it outlasts the end of our work together, and it covers the fact of our involvement as fully as it covers its substance. We would ask the same of you in respect of the methods and written materials we share, which are the firm's own way of working and are meant for your use rather than for wider circulation.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm engaged for it, and we stand behind what we do. We do not, however, control the commercial and organizational decisions that {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} will ultimately take on the strength of our advice, nor the conditions in which those decisions are carried out, and so, save to the extent the law does not permit such a limit, our liability to you arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be determined by the courts of that state. Should any single provision of this letter be held unenforceable, the remainder will stand, unaffected by it.

If this letter reflects the understanding we reached, I would be grateful if you would sign the enclosed copy where indicated below and return it to me, keeping the second copy for your own file; once your signed copy is in hand, Julie Parks will write to fix the first meetings and the opening requests for information, so that we can begin without delay.

To: Deborah Gordon
From: Julie Parks
Re: Opening the {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} organization design engagement

The engagement opens on {{fact:f:E-2011-002.start}}. This memo sets down how we start, so we are in step from the first day. The aim of the opening phase is narrow. We build a clean, agreed picture of how {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} is organized today. We form no view yet on how it should change. Nothing in this phase is a recommendation. It is the base the design work stands on, and it has to be solid before we build on it. The five workstreams below run in parallel, but the map comes first, because the others read off it.
The opening phase

items: Current-state org map. Document the reporting lines, the spans of control, and the layers between the top of the house and the front line.
Roles and responsibilities. Record what each manager is accountable for, and where two managers believe they own the same thing.
Decision rights. Trace how a handful of everyday decisions actually travel, and mark where authority is unclear or sits away from the work.
Interviews. Sit with the managers who run each function, so the map rests on how the work is done and not only on the chart.
Benchmarks. Set the spans and layers against a sensible reference, so we can see where the structure is heavy and where it is thin.

blocks.text: You own the map and the benchmarks. Work from the client's own charts and job descriptions first, then close the gaps in the interviews. Where the chart and the interviews disagree, keep the note close to the evidence and flag it. We do not tidy a discrepancy away; a discrepancy is often the finding.

Our sponsor on the client side is Julie Gonzalez, the Director of Operations. Route every request for data and access through her, so {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} hears one voice from us. She has asked that anything we need in the first month reach her as a single consolidated note. That is sensible. Plan the requests once, rather than send them as they occur to us.

Two dependencies decide the pace. The first is access to the managers. The interviews are where the map earns its keep, and a week of unavailable calendars is a week the phase does not move. The second is the client's own charts. If they are current we start from them; if they are stale we rebuild the reporting lines from the interviews, which is slower. Flag either one to me the moment it slips, not at the review.

On cadence, you and I keep a short standing check-in each week: fifteen minutes, on what is blocked and nothing else. Anything that needs Julie Gonzalez to decide, bring to me first and I will take it to her. Keep the shared engagement file current, so neither of us is working from a private copy.

The test of a finished opening phase is simple. We can set the present structure on one page, name the two or three places where it costs the business, and point to the evidence behind each. Until we can do that, the phase is not done, whatever the calendar says. First step is the consolidated data request. Draft it by Friday and send it to me, and I will add the client contacts before it goes out.
Good morning Julie,

A short note on where the organization design work stands. Deborah Gordon has the current-state map drafted for the two largest functions, and we walked the early version on Monday. Nothing in it is a conclusion. It shows how the work is directed today, which is what we need settled before we look at what should change.

To close the map I need two things from your side. The first is the current org charts and headcount for the remaining functions, so the picture is complete rather than partial. The second is thirty minutes each with the two managers who run field operations, since the detail behind the reporting lines tends to live with the people who work them. If any of that needs a sign-off, Julie Gonzalez, tell me who to ask and I will approach them directly rather than put it back on your desk.

Send whatever is easiest straight to me, Julie Parks, and I will keep this thread as the single place these requests and their answers live. If the charts reach us by the middle of next week, we stay comfortably on track for {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}}.
Thanks
Good morning Julie,

Thank you, the charts came through this morning. Deborah Gordon has them and can close the current-state map on the remaining functions this week. That keeps the work for {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}} on schedule.

One point is worth raising while it is still small. The headcount file lists a handful of roles under two managers at once, which is usually where a design question hides rather than a clerical error. It is not urgent, and we can carry it as an open item. If someone on your team can confirm who actually owns those roles, or point Deborah Gordon to where that is written down, we can settle it without a full re-cut.

I would also like a short working session next week to walk you through what the current-state read is showing before we take it wider. Could you, Julie Gonzalez, hold thirty minutes, and I will send a short agenda beforehand so no one reads the exhibits cold. Send the confirmation straight to me, Julie Parks, and I will set it up.
Thanks
Organization Design for {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}}

An interim briefing for the leadership team. The engagement opened on {{fact:f:E-2011-002.start}} and is in its early weeks. This is a read of where the work stands and what we are examining, not a set of conclusions; those come later, and only once the evidence behind them is settled with your people.
Where the Work Stands

Nothing here is a recommendation. The design work follows once the present picture is settled.
Deborah Gordon has the map drafted for the two largest functions and is closing the remainder.
Today is about sharing what we are examining and agreeing the questions worth pursuing.

blocks.text: Working Session Minutes

These minutes record the working session we held on the organization design engagement for {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}}, at which the engagement team and the client reviewed the current-state read and settled the questions the design work will take up next. They set down who was with us, what we discussed, and the actions each side agreed to carry before we meet again.
Present

items: Julie Parks, Senior Engagement Manager, Calderwood Partners (chair)
Deborah Gordon, Associate, Calderwood Partners
Julie Gonzalez, Director of Operations, {{fact:f:E-2011-002.client}}

blocks.text: Discussion

I walked the group through the current-state read, which is now substantially complete across the largest functions and under way on the rest. My account was that the reporting lines hold together cleanly within each function taken on its own, but that the picture changes at the seams between functions, where the same responsibility is claimed by two managers and, in a couple of places, by none. Julie Parks was careful to have us treat this as an observation drawn from the charts and the interviews rather than as a criticism of anyone.

We spent most of the hour on spans and layers, and in particular on where the structure has grown heavier than the work requires. Julie Gonzalez confirmed the pattern from her own vantage and noted that several of the reporting lines had been added in stages as the business grew, with the result that a few managers now carry a span of one or two people while others carry far more than they can attend to. We agreed that the design should separate the layers that exist to do the work from those that exist only to relieve a title, since a recommendation that ignored that distinction would not survive contact with the operation.

One question we left open by agreement. Julie Parks set out the choice plainly: the design can either redraw a single function end to end as a demonstration, which is the more contained course and the easier to adjust should the managers push back, or it can take up the cross-cutting decision rights at once, which is the more ambitious course and the harder to reverse. No one pressed for a decision in the room, since the call belongs to the client's leadership and we will bring it to them framed as a choice rather than as the firm's conclusion.
Actions

rows: Close the current-state read on the remaining functions and schedule the two outstanding interviews
Confirm which roles are claimed by two managers at once, and which by none
Frame the single-function-versus-cross-cutting choice as a short decision paper for leadership

blocks.text: The item that gates our next session is the second action, since until we know where the responsibilities genuinely sit we cannot separate what the design can settle now from what has to wait; once Julie Gonzalez's team has confirmed those, I will circulate a first outline of the design options ahead of the meeting.
